 Valve Won't "Be Gatekeepers" by Banning AI Games, As "AI Slop" Complaints Grow 
 by Cpt.Jank 
 Yesterday, 12:15
 Discuss (21 Comments) 
 Valve has a growing AI problem on its storefront, and it's not only that game developers are using AI, which is a point of contention for many gamers but not necessarily the biggest concern for developers. Instead, game developers are increasingly reporting that their games are being cloned by developers using AI to clone games from short demos or PR materials ahead of the original game's launch. There has also been an outcry over the number of low-effort AI-generated or AI-assisted games bringing down the overall quality of Steam Next Fest. As reported by Inven , during a recent panel at the Steam Indie Connect developer event, Valve's Tom Giardino and Marc Wilkinson addressed some of these concerns by developers. Tom Giardino via Inven We don't want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use...Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy, you need to keep growing your game by adding features, personality, and creativity that stem from your own perspective Giardino's, and seemingly Valve's, stance on AI game cloning is rather lax in the sense that it appears to mostly leave it up to developers to combat those clones by being more competitive. He explains that game clones have always existed, as has chasing trendy concepts and game mechanics during events like Next Fest, even if AI has made these issues more prevalent by making games easier to clone. He advised that developers take a two-pronged approach to dealing with those clones, first building a community and an identity for their game via an online presence, community engagement and building trust. The second step in combating game clones is for developers to continuously improve their games. 
When asked about instances of extortion faced by developers, in which bad actors cloned a game and threatened the developer with releasing it before the original if money wasn't paid to the extortionist, Giardino expressed concern, stating that this was the first time he had heard of such a case, but encouraged developers to report those cases to Valve. If you report such cases to us, we want to look into them further and help in whatever way we can. When directly asked about low-quality games flooding Steam Next Fest, which can result in games getting lost in the noise, Marc Wilkinson explained that recommendation system for Next Fest is based on randomized visibility for the first two days, with the following days being based on personalized recommendations. He goes on to explain that the random exposure was put in place in order to ensure fairness and avoid larger developers taking advantage of the recommendation system. That said, he also acknowledged that Valve is working on addressing Steam's game visibility issue, but that it's challenging, because each studio has a different standard for success; where a small indie developer might be over the moon about 10,000 new wishlists during Next Fest, 10× that amount might still fall short for someone like EA or Ubisoft. We recognize that the trade-off is some low-quality games get exposed. We are fully aware of the situation, and a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve this problem.
